content:
Shares in Advanced Micro Devices fell sharply on Thursday after a short-selling firm accused the chipmaker of deep business ties to China, including claims that a blacklisted Chinese server maker kept receiving newer versions of AMD firmware long after Washington put it on its export blacklist. The sell-off erased billions of dollars from AMD's market value in a single session and dragged the wider chip sector down with it.

AMD closed down 7.72 percent at $489.19 on November 19, according to [CNBC's market coverage](https://www.tradingview.com/news/cnbctv:cf1e4cb4a094b:0/), after falling as much as 11 percent during the session. The decline continued after the closing bell, with the shares down a further 4.74 percent to around $466 in after-hours trading, and they were down about 6 percent again in premarket trading on Friday, according to [the Economic Times](https://m.economictimes.com/markets/us-stocks/wall-street-guide/amd-shares-fall-6-after-short-seller-hunterbrook-flags-china-ties-echoing-nvidia-concerns/amp_articleshow/136025862.cms).

The trigger was a report published on the morning of November 19 by Hunterbrook Media, a short-selling investment firm that disclosed it had taken a short position in AMD — a bet that profits if the share price falls. Hunterbrook alleged that IEIT Systems, a Chinese server manufacturer added to the US Commerce Department's Entity List in March 2025, continued to incorporate newer versions of AMD firmware into its products after being blacklisted. The Entity List requires exporters to obtain licences for covered shipments, and the Commerce Department's stated policy is to deny such licences to listed companies.

According to Hunterbrook, IEIT incorporated at least six newer versions of AMD's firmware into its products after the blacklisting, with the most recent update posted on October 19. The firmware, the report said, enables AMD chips to run in servers supplied by the Chinese firm. The investigation also identified three companies closely linked to IEIT — Maginfra in China, Kaytus in Singapore and Aivres in California — whose products allegedly used firmware nearly identical to that found in IEIT's servers, suggesting they could be selling servers designed by the blacklisted company. Hunterbrook cited corporate filings linking Aivres and Kaytus to IEIT.

AMD rejected the allegations. "The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," a company spokesperson said in a statement, adding that AMD "complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations." CNBC, which first reported the story, said it had not independently verified Hunterbrook's information.

Crucially, Hunterbrook itself acknowledged the limits of its own findings. The firm wrote that it "does not know how IEIT obtained AMD's code, or whether AMD or anyone else held a license to supply it," and that the records it found "don't establish on their own a violation of export laws." That caveat, buried in the report, did little to slow the sell-off — but it matters, because it means the investigation has not established that AMD directly supplied restricted technology to IEIT or broke US rules.

The report went further, alleging broader exposure to China. Hunterbrook claimed that more than 20 percent of AMD's revenue was billed to customers in China and Hong Kong, and that the chipmaker depends on a Chinese partner, Tongfu Microelectronics, to finish most of its chips. According to the report, two ventures that are 85 percent owned by Tongfu provide the majority of AMD's chip assembly, testing and packaging services, with AMD holding the remaining 15 percent and having extended a $100 million loan to one of the ventures, still outstanding at the end of September.

Hunterbrook also flagged a regulatory risk on the horizon. It said a rule extending export restrictions to foreign companies at least 50 percent owned by blacklisted entities could come into effect after its current suspension expires on January 10, 2027 — a change that, if adopted, could place further limits on AMD's international business.

Chief executive Lisa Su, who has led AMD since 2014, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China remained an "important" market for the company, while stressing that AMD intended to remain fully compliant with US export controls. Attention has also fallen on Su's own share sales: she sold 640,000 shares for about $248 million this year, including $35.5 million worth on November 16, three days before Hunterbrook's report. A filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission shows the November 16 sale was made under a pre-arranged Rule 10b5-1 trading plan adopted on June 8, 2026, and the available information does not establish that Su knew about the report in advance or that the sale was connected to its publication.

The episode comes as the chip industry faces widening scrutiny over China links. Nvidia, the sector's dominant company, is facing investigations over sales to companies in Asia with links to China, and AMD had previously been seen as a potential beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding its rival. [A US congressional report this month](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/us-congress-report-china-nvidia-chips-ai-weapons-november-2026) raised separate concerns about Nvidia chips reaching Chinese military-linked uses, underscoring how export controls have become a central fault line for the whole industry.

The AMD sell-off also fed into a broader market rout. [Global stocks were heading for their worst run in more than three years](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/global-stocks-worst-run-since-2023-ai-selloff-november-2026) as a sharp sell-off in artificial intelligence shares spread from Wall Street across Asia, with the MSCI All Country World Index on course for a seventh consecutive day of declines.

What happens next will turn on two things. First, whether US regulators take any interest in the IEIT firmware question — so far there is no indication of an investigation into AMD. Second, whether Washington proceeds with the tougher ownership-based export rule in January, which could reshape how American chipmakers structure their overseas supply chains. Until then, investors are left weighing an unproven allegation from a firm that profits if AMD's shares fall against a company that insists it follows the rules — and a share price that has already rendered its verdict for the week.
summary: AMD shares plunged 7.7% after short seller Hunterbrook alleged a blacklisted Chinese server maker kept receiving newer AMD firmware. AMD rejected the claims, and Hunterbrook itself admitted it could not show how the code was obtained or prove a violation.
title: AMD shares plunge after short seller alleges blacklisted Chinese firm kept getting its firmware
